answer.evidence: The whole building is a flat south facade with no roof slope, no ellipse, and no visible horizontal surface. The top is a 3-4 row parapet band (rows 6-9) that reads as a rim. The cornice at rows 38-42 and the ledge at rows 70-74 are front-facing strips without a distinct top plane or eave shadow. The window awnings are thin vertical strips. Everything else (windows, sign, shopfront glass, wall bricks) is a vertical face, so the drawing is a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a modern grey-concrete post office with a red sign. Its outlines are tinted (0% near-neutral edge pixels), a dark blue-grey beside the walls and panels, so they are dark material tone rather than sticker black. Visible tones per tile are 9, against 12 and 10 for the references, so it is close to the stone reference but below h101. Near-flat coverage is 20% against 0% for both references. The flat areas are the rooftop panel, the upper wall band, the red sign and the storefront frame. The brick courses on the wall have some grain and the windows have gradient reflections, but the walls and sign read as 3-4 step ramps rather than the 5-6 steps Beodeul uses on its materials. There is no per-tile scalloping or speckle of the kind the roofs and plaster carry in the references. The piece is cleanly drawn and not sticker-like, but it is flatter and shallower than the references, with flat fills and fewer shading steps.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a modern grey-concrete post office with a flat rooftop, air-conditioner units and a red sign. It is the same kind (a whole building), but it is drawn with a different construction than the Beodeul houses. Its outlines are tinted dark blue-grey and not neutral black (0% near-neutral dark edge pixels), so they read as dark material tone. The brick grain on the walls, the glass panes with highlights and the sign lettering give some texture. Even so, large parts are flat. The rooftop panel, the wall bands and the sign face are almost uniform fills, and near-flat coverage is 20% against 0% on both references. Visible tones per tile are 9 against 12 and 10 for the references, so density is a little lower, not far below. The references show tile-by-tile scallops, per-stone shading and timber grain. This candidate lacks that fine per-element variation, so a careful artist would see it as flatter and slightly thinner next to them.
